name: interface-design
description: Opinionated craft guidance for web, UI, and interaction design, and the content, logos, and illustrations that go with them. Covers hierarchy, typography, color and dark mode, layout, components, states, forms, motion and SVG animation, logos and favicons, content design (build only what was asked, write less, never invent facts), accessibility, and critique. Ships contrast and type-scale scripts and a design-token stylesheet. Use this skill whenever you build, restyle, or review anything people will look at or click (websites, landing pages, web apps, dashboards, forms, sign-up pages, components, HTML/CSS/Tailwind/React front-end work, prototypes) or make a logo, icon, favicon, or animated SVG, even if the user never says "design" (for example "build a signup page", "make this look professional", "why does this feel off?", "make a logo for my shop", "animate this illustration"). Also use it for UX reviews, interface copy, design tokens, palettes, and accessibility.
---

# Interface Design

Good interfaces come from a small number of deliberate decisions applied with discipline, not from decoration. Most weak design isn't ugly so much as *undecided*: five grays where three would do, every element at the same volume, spacing picked per element instead of from a system, states nobody designed. This skill is about making those decisions on purpose, and making them well.

## The stance

- **How it works comes first, then how it looks.** A screen is a tool for someone to get something done. Start from the person and the job, and let the visuals express the hierarchy of that job.
- **Content first.** Design with real or realistic content. Lorem ipsum and "Feature One" hide every real problem: long names, empty lists, three-line titles, seven-digit numbers.
- **Restraint is the default; emphasis is earned.** If everything is bold, nothing is. Every extra color, weight, border, shadow, or animation must justify itself by communicating something.
- **Build what was asked, in as few words as do the job.** Unrequested sections, features, and paragraphs are the most common way generated interfaces go wrong. Invented facts (prices, policies, statistics, testimonials, customer logos) are worse than gaps, because they look finished and get shipped. Offer extras in your reply instead of building them.
- **Quiet almost everywhere, memorable somewhere.** Restraint alone produces competent, forgettable work. Every piece of work gets one signature element tied to the brief (an illustration or product visual made for it, a confident typographic gesture, an ownable color, a beautifully made empty state, a delightful core interaction), and everything around it stays disciplined so it lands. "Clean and modern" is not a direction.
- **Systems over one-offs.** Choose scales (type, space, color, radius, motion) and use only values from them. Consistency is what makes plain things look designed.
- **Specific beats generic.** The generic version of anything (gradient hero, three emoji feature cards, "Unlock your potential") is invisible. Make choices particular to this product and audience.
- **The existing system wins.** Inside a product with an established design language (tokens, component library, Tailwind config, brand guide), follow it even where you'd choose differently; coherence beats personal taste. Point out problems; don't silently "fix" the system.

## Workflow

### 1. Understand before drawing
Work out, mostly by inference (ask only when the answer would materially change the design and you can't infer it):
- **What exactly was asked?** List it, plus what the page needs in order to work (a submit button, a confirmation, error states). That's the scope. Anything else needs a reason the user would agree with.
- **Who** uses this, how often, on what device, in what state of mind? A daily-use admin tool wants density and speed; a once-a-year tax form wants guidance and reassurance.
- **What is the one primary job** of this screen, and what are the secondary ones?
- **What content** exists, how big can it get, and what does it look like empty?
- **What constraints** exist: codebase, component library, brand, framework?

In a codebase, look before you design: find the theme (tailwind.config, CSS custom properties, theme files), the existing components, and a couple of representative screens, then reuse them.

### 2. Choose a direction (new work only)
Decide the personality in one sentence ("a calm, precise tool for accountants"; "a warm, editorial magazine for home cooks"), then commit to the foundational decisions that follow from it:

1. Typeface(s): usually one family, at most two.
2. Neutral temperature: cool, warm, or pure gray.
3. One accent color, and what it means.
4. Corner radius and depth strategy (borders, shadows, or tonal surfaces).
5. Density and base text size.
6. Motion character: none, snappy, or soft.

**Find the direction in the brief, not in a list of things to avoid.** Write down three concrete things from the product's world (its materials, places, objects, era, the people who use it, the name itself) and let them choose the palette, the type, and one signature element. A tea importer might take oxidized green, rice paper, and brushy lettering; a payroll tool for restaurants might take kitchen-ticket monospace and tomato red. Swapping one default for another is not a direction: generic blue-and-white SaaS is a default too, and so is whatever palette you reach for first on every brief. Warmth and character are good when they come from the brief. For calibration, `assets/examples/` has two finished pages in deliberately different directions.

`references/aesthetic-directions.md` has eight worked directions with these filled in. Start from one rather than the no-decision default (Inter everywhere, indigo accent, 12px radius, soft shadows, everything centered), which reads as "template" instantly. For substantial new work, tell the user the direction in a line or two so they can redirect early.

Encode the decisions as tokens. `assets/tokens.css` is a complete starter: change its DECISIONS block, and the palette, radii, and density follow.

### 3. Structure before style
Lay out hierarchy and grouping first: what matters most, what belongs together, what order people read in. Get it working in near-grayscale with real content. If the hierarchy doesn't read without color, color won't save it.

### 4. Apply the system
Fill in type, color, and surfaces from the tokens only. When you reach for an off-scale value, either the scale is missing a step (add it deliberately) or you're compensating for a structural problem (fix the structure).

### 5. Design every state
Default, hover, focus-visible, active, disabled, loading, empty, error, success, and overflow (long text, many items, huge numbers). Unhandled states are where interfaces feel broken. See `references/interaction.md`.

### 6. Look at it, then critique it
If you can render (browser tools, Playwright, screenshots), do it at ~375px, ~768px, and ~1440px wide, in dark mode if supported. This step is not optional polish. Rendering routinely catches what careful reading of the code misses: a selector silently overriding another's font size, grid children stretching to fill a row, colors clipping out of gamut and shifting hue, a fill that passes contrast in light mode and fails in dark, identifiers wrapping mid-word on a phone. Squint at it. Tab through it. Then run the checklist below, or the full method in `references/critique.md`, and fix the biggest problems first. Then read every sentence on the page and delete the ones that restate a heading, invent a fact, or just cheer. When the structure is right, do a polish pass with `references/craft-details.md`.

## Core principles

### Hierarchy
- Each view has one primary focus and one primary action. Decide what they are before styling anything.
- Use the fewest levers: size, weight, color/contrast, position, space. Two together are usually enough.
- **De-emphasize to emphasize.** Make secondary things smaller, lighter, or muted before making the important thing bigger.
- Values often matter more than labels. In "Revenue: $48,210", the number is the content; the label can be small and muted.
- Squint test: blur your eyes. What pops out first should be what matters most.

### Spacing and layout
- A 4px-based scale (4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 48, 64, 96, 128) for every gap, padding, and margin. No 13px or 22px.
- **Proximity encodes relationship:** space within a group must be clearly smaller than space between groups. A label sits closer to its own field than to the previous one.
- Start with more whitespace than feels necessary and remove it. Cramped is worse than airy for everything except expert data tools.
- Align to few edges. Left-align text by default; center only short standalone moments (hero headline, empty state, auth card).
- Constrain widths: prose at ~65ch, forms at 400–640px. Never let content stretch across a 1920px screen.
- Group with the weakest cue that works: space → alignment → background tint → divider → box. Boxes inside boxes are a smell.

### Typography
- One family is usually enough; two at most. Variety comes from size and weight.
- A type scale with distinct steps; most screens need 4–6 sizes. Body 16px on the web (14px is fine in dense apps).
- Leading ~1.5 for body, 1.1–1.25 for headings. Bigger type gets tighter leading and tighter tracking; uppercase labels get positive tracking.
- Two or three weights: 400 for text, 500–600 for labels and headings. App headings are smaller than you think.
- `tabular-nums` for numbers that align or change. `text-wrap: balance` on headings.

### Color
- Neutrals do ~90% of the work. One accent marks action, selection, and focus. Status colors appear only for status.
- Build ramps in OKLCH so steps are perceptually even; tint neutrals slightly. `scripts/color.py ramp` generates them.
- Components use role tokens (`--color-text-muted`, `--color-surface-raised`), never raw hex values or ramp steps.
- Contrast: text ≥ 4.5:1, large text and UI boundaries (input borders, icons, focus rings) ≥ 3:1. Verify with `scripts/color.py contrast`. Light-gray text is the most common failure in otherwise good design.
- Never rely on color alone. Pair it with text, icons, or shape.
- Dark mode is its own palette, not an inversion: dark gray canvas, lighter surfaces for elevation, softened accents, off-white text.

### Surfaces and depth
- Use one separation technique per level: a border *or* a shadow, not both at full strength.
- Shadows are soft, layered, low-opacity, and lit from one direction. If you clearly see a shadow, it's too strong.
- Elevation means something: floating things are temporary or interactive (menus, dialogs). Resting content stays flat.
- Nested radii are concentric: inner = outer − padding. Keep one radius logic across the product.

### Interaction
- Interactive things look interactive and respond within 100ms.
- Visible keyboard focus everywhere (`:focus-visible`, 2px ring, offset, ≥ 3:1). Never remove outlines without a replacement.
- Touch targets ≥ 44×44px; nothing essential hidden behind hover.
- Prefer undo to "Are you sure?". Confirm only irreversible, destructive actions, and name the action on the button ("Delete project").
- Feedback is immediate, proportional, and local to the action.
- Forms: labels above fields (never placeholder-as-label), validate on blur, keep submit enabled and explain what's missing, use correct `type` and `autocomplete`.
- Motion is functional and fast: 150–250ms for most UI, ease-out for entrances, quicker exits, and `prefers-reduced-motion` respected.

### Content: scope, facts, and words
- **Build only what was asked, plus what it needs to work.** A single-purpose page (a form, a sign-up, a confirmation, a 404) gets one column, one action, and no marketing sections: no countdowns, FAQs, testimonial strips, or "why us" cards unless requested.
- **Never invent facts:** prices, fees, cancellation or refund policies, guarantees, trust badges ("Certified experts"), statistics, ratings, testimonials, customer logos, schedules, what a service includes. They hide in fine print as easily as in headlines. Leave them out, or use an unmistakable placeholder and list it in your reply.
- **Sample data uses fictional people and companies,** never real brands as customers or clients. Don't preselect answers people must give (attendance, consent, plan).
- **Cut filler:** paired slogans ("A little X. A lot of Y.", "Less X. More Y."), eyebrow labels that restate the heading below them, taglines under logos, buttons, and in footers, cheerleading inside tools ("You're doing great"), and promo cards nobody asked for. Delete a sentence; if no information is lost, it stays deleted.
- **Buttons say what happens:** "Send invite", "Export report", "Save changes". Avoid "Submit", "Yes/No", and "Click here"; "OK" only for a plain acknowledgment.
- **Sentence case** for all UI text. Specific over grand: "3 files uploaded", not "Your upload was successful!"
- **Errors** say what happened and how to fix it, next to the problem, without blame.

- **Discipline cuts words, claims, sections, and features, not identity.** Imagery, illustration, and typographic character that are about the product stay. Cut the slogan, keep the illustration. A headline with a point of view ("Bookkeeping for people who'd rather be making things") isn't filler; a line that could sit on any site ("Everything you need, all in one place") is.

`references/content-design.md` has the full method and a worked example of a cluttered page versus a considered one.

## Generic tells to avoid

These signal that nothing was decided. Each needs a real reason to appear:
- Indigo/violet accents; purple-to-pink gradients; gradient text; glowing blurred blobs.
- Every section as centered heading + subtitle + three identical cards; emoji or icons-in-circles as decoration.
- A pill badge above every hero headline; "Unlock / Supercharge / Seamless / Revolutionize" copy; triplet slogans.
- The same large radius and soft shadow on everything; cards that scale up on hover; everything fading in on scroll.
- Low-contrast gray text, everything centered, uniform sizes with no hierarchy.
- Today's generated-page tics: an uppercase eyebrow label above every heading, the same italic-serif accent word trick in every headline, "Less X. More Y." headlines, tilted sticker badges, notification cards floating over hero images. Used once, deliberately, any of these can be a signature; repeated everywhere, they're a template.
- Inside apps: upsell cards, motivational lines, decorative illustrations in the sidebar, a slogan under the page title.

The fix is never more style. It's a specific choice: a typeface with character, a real product screenshot, a layout that follows the content, copy that says something only this product could say. `references/critique.md` has the full list, a symptom → cause table, and two worked before → after redesigns that show this judgment in action. Read them when you want calibration.

## Two short examples of deciding

**"Build a settings page for our project-management app"** (existing codebase with Tailwind and a component library). Read the existing theme and components and reuse them. Use a single centered column (~640px), with sections titled "Profile", "Notifications", and "Danger zone", each with a one-line description. Labels go above fields. Notification toggles take effect immediately (switches); profile fields have a Save button (no switches there). Delete workspace lives in the danger zone, opens a confirmation that requires typing the workspace name, and its button says "Delete workspace". Cover the states: saving, saved, validation errors, and a failed save with retry.

**"Make a landing page for a meal-planning app for busy parents"** (new, no brand). Direction: warm and human. Fraunces for headlines and Figtree for text; warm neutrals (`--neutral-h: 70`); a tomato/terracotta accent (`--accent-h: 35`, `--accent-c: 0.14`); 14px radius; comfortable density; soft, quick motion. The hero headline says the outcome plainly ("Dinner, decided. Every week, in five minutes."), with a real-looking plan screenshot rather than an abstract graphic. Sections vary: a split hero, a three-step "how it works" with app screenshots, a single large testimonial slot clearly marked as a placeholder for a real customer quote, pricing, FAQ. No gradients, no emoji icons.

## Pre-ship checklist

- [ ] One clear primary action per view; the squint test matches importance.
- [ ] Spacing, type sizes, colors, radii, and shadows all come from tokens/scales.
- [ ] Text ≥ 4.5:1, UI boundaries and focus ≥ 3:1, in every theme.
- [ ] Prose ≤ ~75ch; headings balanced; numbers tabular where they align.
- [ ] Hover, focus-visible, active, disabled, and loading states on interactive elements.
- [ ] Empty, loading, error, and overflow states designed with realistic content.
- [ ] Works at 375px with no horizontal scroll; targets ≥ 44px; nothing hover-only.
- [ ] Keyboard: logical order, visible focus, Escape closes overlays, focus returns.
- [ ] Semantic HTML: buttons act, links navigate, inputs have labels, headings in order.
- [ ] Motion purposeful and short; reduced-motion respected.
- [ ] Nothing unrequested: no extra sections, features, or promo cards. Extras are offered in the reply instead.
- [ ] No invented facts anywhere, including fine print: prices, fees, policies, guarantees, trust badges, statistics, testimonials, real brands as sample data.
- [ ] Every sentence carries information. Copy is specific, sentence case, with verb buttons; no filler slogans or taglines.
- [ ] Tables and other wide content scroll inside their own container (`overflow-x: auto; position: relative`, so hidden labels inside can't widen the page), or reflow, on a phone.
- [ ] No generic tells left without a reason, including the tics above.
- [ ] One signature element tied to the brief, so the page couldn't be mistaken for a template with the logo swapped.
- [ ] Logos: a version for dark backgrounds, no tagline in the primary mark, a mark redrawn to be legible at 16px.
- [ ] Animation: one idea, small but visible movement, and a complete still frame under reduced motion.

## Reference files

Read what the task needs; don't load everything.

| File | Read when |
|---|---|
| `references/aesthetic-directions.md` | starting new work; choosing a visual personality; font pairings by mood; adapting a brand |
| `references/typography.md` | choosing fonts, type scales, fluid type, font loading, text-heavy pages |
| `references/color.md` | building a palette, theming, dark mode, contrast problems, gradients |
| `references/layout-and-spacing.md` | page and screen layout, grids, widths, density, responsive behavior, surfaces and elevation, radius |
| `references/components.md` | specific components (buttons, inputs, tables, dialogs, nav, cards, menus, toasts, empty states), with CSS recipes |
| `references/interaction.md` | states, feedback, loading, errors, forms behavior, navigation, keyboard, touch, microcopy |
| `references/motion.md` | transitions and animation: durations, easing, choreography, CSS recipes |
| `references/web-design.md` | websites, landing pages, heroes, pricing, editorial and docs pages, web performance |
| `references/accessibility.md` | any production UI; WCAG 2.2 AA; ARIA patterns; testing |
| `references/critique.md` | reviewing a design or screenshot; "make it look better"; diagnosing what feels off; self-review; worked before → after examples |
| `references/craft-details.md` | the polish pass: the small type, color, edge, optical, and interaction details that separate good from great |
| `references/implementation.md` | putting tokens into Tailwind v4/v3, shadcn/ui, other component libraries, React components, or single-file HTML |
| `references/platforms.md` | native iOS/Android conventions, mobile web specifics, tablets |
| `references/content-design.md` | any page with copy, and always for single-purpose pages and landing pages: deciding scope, writing UI text, avoiding invented facts and filler |
| `references/logo-design.md` | designing a logo, wordmark, monogram, app icon, or favicon |
| `references/svg-animation.md` | SVG illustrations, empty-state art, loaders, animated icons, success animations |

## Bundled tools

- `assets/tokens.css`: a starter token stylesheet with OKLCH neutral and accent ramps generated from a hue and chroma, semantic color roles for light and dark (contrast-checked for every accent hue), type, space, size, radius, shadow, motion, and z-index scales, plus a small base reset. Copy it into the project and change the DECISIONS block. Shipping it unchanged everywhere would make everything look alike, which is the opposite of the point.
- `scripts/color.py`: `contrast FG BG` (WCAG 2 ratio + APCA Lc with verdicts), `ramp --hue H --chroma C` (a gamut-mapped 50–950 OKLCH ramp with text-contrast notes; `--format css`), and `convert COLOR` (hex ↔ oklch). Standard-library Python.
- `scripts/scale.py`: modular type scales with suggested line-heights and tracking; fluid `clamp()` values between two viewport widths (`--max-base`/`--max-ratio`); `--space --min --max` for one fluid value like section padding.

- `assets/examples/`: complete exemplar pages built on tokens.css, each in a different direction, with the decisions explained in comments: `app-triage.html` (a dense, keyboard-first work tool, light and dark) and `editorial-article.html` (a long read with a drop cap and margin notes). Open them for calibration on what finished work looks like. Study the decisions; don't copy the look.
- `assets/specimen.html`: a living specimen of tokens.css (type scale, ramps, surfaces, buttons in every state, form fields, settings switches, stat cards, a table, alerts, a toast, an empty state) with live accent-hue, neutral-hue, radius, and theme controls. Open it beside tokens.css when tuning a direction; it doubles as a reference for what "done" looks like at the component level.

Run scripts with `python3 <this-skill-dir>/scripts/<name>.py --help`.

For charts, use a dedicated data-viz skill if one is available; `references/components.md` covers the basics otherwise.

# Interaction design

Visual design gets attention; interaction design determines whether the thing works. The craft is anticipating what a person is trying to do, what they expect to happen, and what they'll need when it doesn't go to plan.

## Contents
1. Principles that hold everywhere
2. Response time and perceived speed
3. The state inventory
4. Feedback
5. Loading
6. Errors: prevent, then explain
7. Forms
8. Destructive actions, undo, and confirmation
9. Navigation and wayfinding
10. Progressive disclosure and defaults
11. Keyboard and power users
12. Touch, pointer, and hover
13. Selection, bulk actions, drag and drop
14. Notifications and interruptions
15. Onboarding and empty states
16. Microcopy
17. Laws worth knowing

---

## 1. Principles that hold everywhere

- **Visibility of state.** People should always be able to tell what's going on: what's selected, what's saving, what failed, where they are.
- **Signifiers.** Things that can be acted on must look like it. Buttons look pressable, links look like links, draggable things have handles, editable fields look editable. Flat, borderless "is this clickable?" design pushes the burden onto users.
- **Feedback.** Every action gets an immediate, proportional response.
- **Mapping.** Controls relate to their effects spatially and conceptually. The control sits next to the thing it changes; up means more.
- **Constraints.** Make invalid actions impossible rather than erroring after the fact (a date picker that can't select past dates for a booking).
- **Consistency.** The same action works and looks the same everywhere, and platform conventions are followed (Jakob's law: people spend most of their time in *other* products).
- **Forgiveness.** Easy to undo, hard to do irreversible damage, and input is never lost.
- **Recognition over recall.** Show options rather than making people remember them: recent items, autocomplete, visible commands, examples in empty fields.

## 2. Response time and perceived speed

| Delay | Perception | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| < 100ms | instant | direct manipulation, hover and press states, toggles |
| 100ms–1s | noticeable, flow intact | subtle pending state; no spinner needed under ~300ms |
| 1–10s | waiting | show progress: skeletons, spinners, labels ("Saving…") |
| > 10s | attention lost | determinate progress, time estimate, let them leave and notify on completion |

Making it feel fast:
- **Optimistic UI:** apply the change immediately (toggle flips, item appears, message sends) and reconcile with the server in the background, rolling back with a clear message if it fails. Use it when success is very likely and the action is reversible.
- **Show content progressively:** render what you have and stream in the rest. Keep stale data visible while revalidating instead of blanking the screen.
- **Avoid spinner flashes:** delay showing a loading indicator by ~200–300ms, and once shown, keep it at least ~400–500ms so it doesn't flicker.
- **Prefetch** likely next steps on hover/intent; preload the next page of results.
- **Never block input while saving** if the save can happen in the background.

## 3. The state inventory

Most interfaces are designed only in their ideal state. Real use is mostly the other states. Design all of them.

**Every interactive element:**
| State | Notes |
|---|---|
| Default | looks interactive |
| Hover | subtle change (background, border, underline) on pointer devices; never the only signifier |
| Focus-visible | strong, unmistakable ring for keyboard users |
| Active / pressed | immediate response on press (darker, slightly inset) |
| Selected / checked / current | persistent, distinct from hover |
| Disabled | visibly inert; explain why if it's not obvious |
| Loading / pending | after activation, while waiting |
| Error / invalid | for inputs |

**Every view or data-driven component:**
| State | Notes |
|---|---|
| Ideal | realistic content, not the perfect demo |
| Empty (first use) | explain what goes here and offer the action to create the first item |
| Empty (no results) | say nothing matched, show the query, suggest a way out (clear filters, fix spelling) |
| Empty (cleared) | positive closure ("All caught up") |
| Loading | skeleton matching the final layout |
| Partial | some data loaded, some failed or pending |
| Error | what happened, whether data is safe, how to retry |
| Offline | what still works, what's queued |
| No permission | why, and who can grant access |
| Overflow | very long names, 10,000 items, huge numbers, many tags, narrow containers |

Test overflow on purpose: a username of 40 characters, a title in German, a price of $1,234,567.89, a list with one item and with 500.

## 4. Feedback

- **Proportional:** small actions get small feedback (a checkmark, a color change); big or risky actions get more (a confirmation message, a summary).
- **Local:** show feedback where the action happened. "Saved" next to the field beats a toast in the corner, which beats a banner at the top.
- **Button pending state:** after click, show a spinner or progress label *inside* the button, keep its width fixed (no layout jump), and prevent double submission. Restore it and show the outcome when done.
- **Success** often needs no message at all if the result is visible (the item appeared in the list). Add explicit confirmation when the result happens elsewhere ("Invite sent to sam@…").
- **Toasts** suit brief, non-critical confirmations of actions that happened off-screen, ideally with Undo. They're wrong for errors that need action, because they disappear. They're wrong for anything long, too.
- **Inline status for saves:** "Saving…" → "Saved" → (fade) near the content; "Couldn't save. Retry" if it fails, persisting until resolved.

## 5. Loading

- **Skeletons** for content-heavy layouts: they preview structure and prevent layout shift. Match the real layout's dimensions closely, keep them low-contrast, and use a subtle shimmer or pulse (1.5–2s cycle) or none.
- **Spinners** for small, indeterminate waits in a specific place (a button, a panel refresh). Not full-screen spinners for page loads if you can show the page frame.
- **Progress bars** when the duration is knowable (uploads, multi-step processes). Real progress beats fake progress, and fake progress that stalls at 99% destroys trust.
- **Keep the frame:** navigation, headers, and layout stay put while content loads. Swapping an entire screen for a spinner feels slow and disorienting.
- **Reserve space** for images (`width`/`height` or `aspect-ratio`), ads, embeds, and async components so content doesn't jump. Layout shift causes misclicks.

## 6. Errors: prevent, then explain

**Prevention first:**
- Constrain inputs (pickers, steppers, select lists for closed sets).
- **Be liberal in what you accept:** phone numbers with spaces or dashes, card numbers with spaces, emails with trailing whitespace, dates in several formats. Normalize them silently.
- Sensible defaults; inline hints before the error happens ("8+ characters").
- Disable impossible actions only when the reason is self-evident, otherwise allow the action and explain.

**When errors happen, a good message says:**
1. **What happened**, in plain language (no codes as the main message, no "An error occurred").
2. **Why**, if known and useful.
3. **How to fix it**, or what to do next.
4. Reassurance about data, when relevant ("Your draft is saved").

| Bad | Good |
|---|---|
| Invalid input | Enter a date in the future |
| Error 500 | We couldn't load your invoices. Try again, or check our status page if it keeps happening. |
| Password does not meet requirements | Password needs at least 8 characters (you have 6) |
| Upload failed | That file is 32 MB; the limit is 25 MB. Try compressing it. |

**Placement:**
- **Field errors** inline, directly below (or beside) the field, with an icon and text in the danger color, connected via `aria-describedby`.
- **Form-level summary** at the top for long forms after a failed submit, linking to each field, with focus moved to the summary or first invalid field.
- **Page or system errors** in the area that failed, with retry. Keep the rest of the page usable.
- **Never clear the user's input on error.** Re-typing a long form because one field was wrong is the fastest way to lose someone.
- Don't blame ("You entered an invalid…"). Don't joke in errors that cost people money or data.

## 7. Forms

Forms are where interfaces most often fail people. Good form design is mostly about removing work.

**Structure**
- **Ask for less.** Every field costs completion. Cut what you don't need, defer what you don't need yet, infer what you can (city from postcode, card type from number).
- **Single column.** Multi-column forms cause skipped fields and zig-zag reading, except for tightly related short pairs (first/last name, city/postcode, expiry/CVC).
- **Labels above fields** (fastest to scan, works on mobile, handles long labels). Left-aligned labels to the side only for dense, familiar admin forms.
- **Never use placeholder text as the label.** It disappears on typing, usually fails contrast, and looks like a pre-filled value. Placeholders are for format examples at most.
- **Group related fields** with headings or fieldsets; break long forms into logical steps with a progress indicator.
- **Size fields to their expected input:** a postcode field shouldn't be as wide as an address field. Width is a hint.
- **Mark the minority:** if most fields are required, mark optional ones "(optional)". If most are optional, mark the required ones. An asterisk alone needs explaining.

**Behavior**
- **Validate on blur** (when leaving a field), not on every keystroke; a field shouldn't turn red while someone is still typing their email. Once a field has shown an error, re-validate on input so the error clears as soon as it's fixed.
- **Keep the submit button enabled.** A disabled submit button with no explanation leaves people stuck guessing. Let them submit and show what's missing.
- **Use the right input types and attributes:** `type="email"`, `type="tel"`, `inputmode="numeric"` (for codes, not `type="number"`), `autocomplete` tokens (`email`, `given-name`, `street-address`, `one-time-code`, `new-password`, `cc-number`). Correct attributes enable autofill and the right mobile keyboard, which is the single biggest speed-up for forms.
- **Password fields:** a show/hide toggle; allow paste; state the rules up front; support password managers (`autocomplete="new-password"` or `"current-password"`).
- **Selection controls:** radios for 2–5 mutually exclusive options (all visible), a select or combobox for longer lists, checkboxes for independent choices, a toggle switch only for settings that take effect immediately.
- **Enter submits single-line forms.** Escape cancels in dialogs.
- **Autofocus** the first field only when filling the form is clearly the page's purpose (login, search), never on pages where it would scroll past content or open the mobile keyboard unexpectedly.
- **Preserve progress:** autosave long forms or warn before navigating away with unsaved changes.
- **Primary action at the end of the form,** aligned with the fields' left edge (or right, consistent with your system), labeled with the outcome ("Create account", "Pay $42.00").

## 8. Destructive actions, undo, and confirmation

- **Prefer undo to confirmation.** Confirmation dialogs get clicked through by habit; undo catches the actual mistake. Pattern: perform the action, show a toast "Project archived · Undo" for 5–10 seconds, actually delete later (soft delete).
- **Confirm only when the action is destructive and irreversible**, or costly (sends money, emails 10,000 people).
- **Write confirmations that can be answered without reading the question:** title states the consequence ("Delete 'Q3 report'?"), body says what will be lost ("This permanently deletes the report and its 14 comments."), and the button names the action ("Delete report") in the danger style. The cancel button is plain "Cancel". Never "Are you sure?" with "OK/Cancel" or "Yes/No".
- **For catastrophic actions** (delete an account, a production database), require typing the resource name.
- **Separate destructive controls spatially** from frequent ones (a "Danger zone" section, or the end of a menu after a divider) so they aren't hit by accident.
- Default focus in a destructive confirmation goes to the safe option.

## 9. Navigation and wayfinding

People should always be able to answer: Where am I? What's here? Where can I go? How do I get back?
- **Show location:** highlight the current nav item (not just on hover), use clear page titles matching the nav label, and breadcrumbs for deep hierarchies.
- **The URL is part of the interface:** tabs, filters, sort, search queries, pagination, and open dialogs worth sharing should be reflected in the URL, so Back works, refresh preserves state, and links can be shared.
- **The Back button must do what people expect.** Don't break it with client-side state that isn't in history, and don't add history entries for trivial changes.
- **Preserve scroll position and state** when returning to a list from a detail view.
- **Keep navigation stable:** items don't reorder, appear, or disappear based on context in ways that break muscle memory.
- **Name things by what users call them**, not internal jargon.
- **Links navigate; buttons act.** A link goes somewhere (has a URL, can open in a new tab); a button does something on this page. Don't style or code one as the other.
- **New tabs:** open external links in the same tab by default; use new tabs only when leaving would lose work, and indicate it.

## 10. Progressive disclosure and defaults

- **Show what most people need; reveal the rest on demand.** Advanced settings behind an "Advanced" disclosure, rarely used actions in an overflow menu, details on expand.
- **But don't hide the primary path.** Disclosure is for secondary complexity, not for core actions. Hiding key actions in a "⋯" menu or behind hover makes them undiscoverable.
- **Good defaults are the most powerful design decision.** Most people never change them. Default to the safest and most common choice, pre-fill what you know, and remember the user's last choice.
- **Choice overload (Hick's law):** more options mean slower decisions. Curate. Recommend one option when the choice is hard (the highlighted pricing tier).

## 11. Keyboard and power users

- **Everything works with the keyboard:** logical tab order following the visual order, visible focus, no keyboard traps.
- **Expected keys:** Enter activates/submits, Space toggles/activates buttons, Escape closes the topmost overlay, arrow keys move within composite widgets (menus, tabs, listboxes, grids, radio groups), Home/End jump to the extremes.
- **Focus management:** opening a dialog moves focus into it; closing returns focus to the trigger. After deleting an item, move focus to a sensible neighbor, not back to the top of the page.
- **Shortcuts for frequent actions** in productivity tools (single keys like `C` to create or `/` to search, or modifier combos). Make them discoverable: show them in tooltips and menus, and offer a `?` cheat sheet. Never hijack browser or OS shortcuts (Cmd+F, Cmd+L, Cmd+W).
- **Command palette** (Cmd/Ctrl+K) for apps with many actions: fuzzy search over commands, navigation, and recent items.

## 12. Touch, pointer, and hover

- **Hover doesn't exist on touch.** Anything revealed only on hover (row actions, tooltips with essential info, menus) must have a touch alternative. Use `@media (hover: hover)` for hover-only enhancements.
- **Target size:** at least 24×24px (WCAG 2.2 AA minimum), 44×44px recommended on touch. Small visual elements can have larger hit areas via padding or a pseudo-element.
- **Spacing between targets** prevents mis-taps; dense icon rows need gaps.
- **Thumb reach:** on phones, primary actions near the bottom; destructive actions away from the main thumb path.
- **Gestures need visible alternatives.** Swipe-to-delete needs a visible delete somewhere too; pinch-zoom needs buttons.
- **Hover intent:** menus that open on hover need a short open delay (~100–150ms), a longer close delay (~300ms), and a forgiving path to the submenu (the "safe triangle"). Click-to-open is usually better.
- **Tooltips:** for supplementary labels (icon buttons, truncated text), appear after ~400–700ms on hover and immediately on keyboard focus, and contain no interactive content and nothing essential.
- **Cursor:** `pointer` on clickable non-link elements is conventional on the web; keep it consistent. `not-allowed` for disabled.

## 13. Selection, bulk actions, drag and drop

- **Selection:** checkboxes appear on hover (pointer) or are always visible (touch, or when any item is selected). Shift-click selects ranges. A select-all in the header, with a "Select all 1,240 results" follow-up when paginated.
- **Bulk action bar** appears when items are selected, showing the count ("3 selected") and the available actions, with a way to clear the selection.
- **Drag and drop:** a visible grab handle (⋮⋮) when not obvious; lift the item on drag (shadow, slight scale); show a placeholder where it will land; auto-scroll near edges; animate the drop. Always provide a non-drag alternative (move up/down buttons, a "Move to…" menu) for keyboard and accessibility.

## 14. Notifications and interruptions

Attention is the scarcest resource. Spend it carefully.
- **Interruption ladder**, from least to most intrusive: inline indicator (badge, dot) → inline message → toast → banner → modal → OS notification/email. Use the lowest rung that will do the job.
- **Modals interrupt.** Use them for decisions that block progress or need focused input, not for marketing, tips, or announcements.
- **Banners** for persistent, page- or app-level conditions (trial ending, degraded service, unsaved changes), and they're dismissible unless critical.
- **Badges** for counts that need eventual attention; clear them when the user has seen the content.
- **No pop-ups on arrival** (newsletter modals, cookie walls bigger than needed, chat widgets that open themselves). They're the most hated pattern on the web.

## 15. Onboarding and empty states

- **Empty states are onboarding.** The first time someone sees a feature, its empty state should explain the value in a sentence, show what it will look like (illustration or preview), and offer the one action to begin ("Create your first project"). Sample data or templates help even more.
- **Learn by doing beats tours.** Multi-step coachmark tours get skipped and forgotten. Contextual hints at the moment of need work better.
- **Don't front-load setup.** Let people experience value before asking for profile details, invites, and preferences.
- **Checklists** ("3 of 5 steps done") work for products with genuine setup, and should be dismissible.

## 16. Microcopy

Words are interface. Most UI text is read in fragments, under pressure, mid-task.
- **Buttons are verbs plus objects:** "Save changes", "Create invoice", "Send 3 invites". Not "Submit", "OK", "Yes", or "Click here". A button label should make sense on its own.
- **Match the button to the heading:** a dialog titled "Delete project?" has a "Delete project" button.
- **Sentence case** for everything in UI: buttons, labels, headings, menu items. Title Case Feels Formal And Is Harder To Scan.
- **Be specific and brief:** "3 files uploaded" beats "Your upload was successful!" Remove "please", "simply", "just", "successfully", and exclamation marks.
- **Use the user's vocabulary**, not system internals ("Couldn't connect to the server" over "ECONNREFUSED"; "workspace" if that's what they call it).
- **Talk to the user as "you"** and write as a helpful person would speak. Consistent voice; tone shifts with the situation (lighter for success, plain and calm for errors).
- **Numbers and time:** relative times for recent events ("3 min ago") with the absolute time on hover; absolute dates for anything older than a week; locale-aware formatting; units always shown.
- **Labels describe the value, not the control:** "Email" not "Enter your email".
- **Truncation:** truncate with an ellipsis in the middle for file names and IDs where the end matters (`report-fin…-v3.pdf`), at the end otherwise, and show the full text on hover or focus.

## 17. Laws worth knowing

- **Fitts's law:** time to hit a target depends on its distance and size. Make frequent targets big and close; screen edges and corners are "infinitely" large for mouse users; put a popover's actions near where the pointer already is.
- **Hick's law:** decision time grows with the number of choices. Curate and group options.
- **Jakob's law:** users expect your product to work like the ones they already use. Innovate on value, not on basic conventions (logo links home, cart top-right, Cmd+K opens search in tools).
- **Miller's/chunking:** people handle information in chunks. Group long numbers (card numbers, phone numbers), break long lists into sections.
- **Doherty threshold:** productivity soars when the system responds in under ~400ms.
- **Tesler's law (conservation of complexity):** some complexity can't be removed, only moved. Move it to the system rather than the user.
- **Peak-end rule:** people judge an experience by its most intense moment and its end. Make the finish of a flow (confirmation, success state) feel good.
- **Postel's law:** be liberal in what you accept, conservative in what you send.
- **Aesthetic-usability effect:** people perceive attractive interfaces as easier to use, and forgive them more. Polish isn't superficial.
# Accessibility

Accessibility is a quality bar, not a separate feature. About one in six people worldwide lives with a significant disability (WHO), and everyone is situationally impaired sometimes: bright sunlight, a broken trackpad, a baby in one arm, a slow connection, aging eyes. The practices below make interfaces better for everyone, and most cost nothing if built in from the start.

Target **WCAG 2.2 level AA**. It's the common legal standard and a sensible quality floor.

## Contents
1. The essentials (do these always)
2. Semantic HTML first
3. Keyboard and focus
4. Color, contrast, and visual design
5. Text, zoom, and reflow
6. Images, icons, and media
7. Forms
8. Dynamic content
9. Component patterns
10. Motion and timing
11. Forced colors and user preferences
12. Testing
13. Snippets

---

## 1. The essentials (do these always)

- [ ] Native elements for their purpose: `<button>` for actions, `<a href>` for navigation, `<label>` for inputs, real headings, lists, and tables.
- [ ] Everything operable by keyboard, in a logical order, with a clearly visible focus indicator.
- [ ] Text contrast ≥ 4.5:1 (3:1 for large text); control boundaries, icons, and focus rings ≥ 3:1.
- [ ] Color never the only way information is conveyed.
- [ ] Every image has appropriate alt text (or `alt=""` if decorative); every icon-only button has an accessible name.
- [ ] Every form field has a visible, programmatically associated label; errors are described in text and linked to their field.
- [ ] The page works at 200% zoom and at 320px width without horizontal scrolling (except for things like data tables and maps).
- [ ] `<html lang>`, a descriptive `<title>`, one `<h1>`, headings in order, landmark elements.
- [ ] Respect `prefers-reduced-motion`; nothing flashes more than 3 times per second.
- [ ] Touch targets at least 24×24px (44×44 recommended).

## 2. Semantic HTML first

The first rule of ARIA: don't use ARIA if a native element does the job. Native elements come with keyboard behavior, focus, roles, and states for free.
- `<button>` not `<div onclick>`. A div needs `role="button"`, `tabindex="0"`, and Enter and Space handlers to approximate what a button does natively.
- `<a href>` for anything that navigates. Links without `href` aren't focusable.
- `<nav>`, `<main>`, `<header>`, `<footer>`, `<aside>`, `<section aria-labelledby>` give screen-reader users a map.
- Headings (`h1`–`h6`) form the outline people navigate by. Choose the level by structure and style it however you like; don't skip levels for visual size.
- `<ul>`/`<ol>` for lists (screen readers announce "list, 5 items"), `<table>` with `<th scope>` for tabular data (never for layout).
- `<dialog>`, `<details>/<summary>`, `[popover]`, `<input type="date">`, and `<select>` provide accessible behavior that's hard to replicate.

## 3. Keyboard and focus

- **Tab order follows visual order.** Don't use positive `tabindex`; fix the DOM order instead. `tabindex="0"` makes a custom element focusable; `tabindex="-1"` makes something focusable by script only.
- **Visible focus, always.** Use `:focus-visible` so mouse users don't see rings on click but keyboard users always do. 2px solid, ≥ 3:1 against adjacent colors, with an offset so it doesn't merge with the element's border. Never `outline: none` without a replacement.
- **Focus not obscured** (WCAG 2.2): sticky headers and footers must not cover the focused element; use `scroll-padding-top` equal to header height.
- **No keyboard traps,** except intentional, escapable ones (modal dialogs trap focus until closed with Escape).
- **Manage focus on context change:** move focus into opened dialogs, back to the trigger on close; to the new content's heading after client-side navigation; to a sensible place after deleting an item.
- **Skip link** as the first focusable element: "Skip to main content", visible on focus.
- **Composite widgets** (tabs, menus, listboxes, grids, radio groups, toolbars) use one tab stop and arrow keys inside (roving tabindex or `aria-activedescendant`).

## 4. Color, contrast, and visual design

- Contrast requirements and tooling: see color.md and `scripts/color.py contrast`.
- **Non-text contrast (1.4.11):** input borders, checkbox and radio outlines, toggle tracks, icon buttons without labels, focus indicators, and meaningful chart elements need 3:1 against adjacent colors.
- **Use of color (1.4.1):** links in body text need an underline (or another non-color cue); errors need an icon or text; required fields need a text marker; charts need labels or patterns.
- **Hover and focus content (1.4.13):** tooltips and popovers shown on hover must be dismissible (Escape), hoverable (pointer can move onto them), and persistent until dismissed.
- **Text over images** needs a scrim, overlay, or text shadow sufficient to guarantee contrast at every point.

## 5. Text, zoom, and reflow

- Size text in `rem`, never set a px font size on `html`, and don't disable zoom (`user-scalable=no` / `maximum-scale=1` are failures).
- **200% zoom** (1.4.4): no clipped or overlapping text, no lost functionality.
- **Reflow at 320 CSS px** (1.4.10): content works in a single column without horizontal scrolling.
- **Text spacing** (1.4.12): layouts survive users increasing line height to 1.5, paragraph spacing to 2×, letter spacing to 0.12em, and word spacing to 0.16em. Avoid fixed heights on text containers.
- Avoid text in images; avoid justified text; keep line lengths reasonable.

## 6. Images, icons, and media

- **Alt text** conveys the purpose in context. A product photo: what it shows. A chart: the takeaway ("Revenue grew 40% in Q3"), with the data available elsewhere. A linked image: the destination. Decorative: `alt=""`.
- **Icon-only buttons:** `aria-label="Close"` (or visually hidden text). Decorative icons next to text: `aria-hidden="true"`.
- **SVG icons:** `aria-hidden="true" focusable="false"` when decorative; `role="img"` with `<title>` when meaningful.
- **Video:** captions for speech, audio description or a transcript for important visual content, no autoplay with sound, and controls.
- **Animated GIFs and autoplaying video** need a way to pause.

## 7. Forms

- Every input has a `<label for>` (or wraps it). Placeholders are not labels.
- Group radios and checkboxes in `<fieldset>` with a `<legend>`.
- Helper text and errors are linked with `aria-describedby`; invalid fields get `aria-invalid="true"`.
- Required fields: the `required` attribute plus a visible text marker.
- On failed submit, move focus to an error summary (with links to fields) or the first invalid field.
- `autocomplete` attributes on personal data fields (1.3.5), which also enable autofill.
- **Accessible authentication** (3.3.8): don't block paste in password or code fields; support password managers; don't rely on cognitive tests (puzzles, memorization).
- **Redundant entry** (3.3.7): don't make people re-enter information they already provided in the same process.

## 8. Dynamic content

- **Live regions** announce changes that happen without focus moving: `role="status"` (polite: "Saved", "3 results") and `role="alert"` (assertive: errors that need immediate attention). The region must exist in the DOM before content is inserted into it.
- **Toasts** need a live region and enough time to read (or no timeout for important content); don't put the only copy of an action in a disappearing toast.
- **Loading:** `aria-busy="true"` on the region being updated; announce completion if it isn't obvious.
- **Client-side routing:** update `document.title`, move focus to the new page's `h1` (or announce the navigation).
- **Infinite scroll** traps keyboard users above the footer. Provide "Load more" or pagination.

## 9. Component patterns

Follow the WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices Guide (APG) for custom widgets. Key points:
- **Dialog:** native `<dialog>` + `showModal()`. Label it (`aria-labelledby` pointing to the title). Escape closes; focus returns to the trigger.
- **Disclosure/accordion:** `<details>/<summary>`, or a `<button aria-expanded aria-controls>` toggling a region.
- **Tabs:** `role="tablist"`, `role="tab"` with `aria-selected`, `role="tabpanel"`; arrow keys move between tabs.
- **Menu button:** `<button aria-haspopup="menu" aria-expanded>`. Use `role="menu"` only for application-style action menus, never for site navigation (use a list of links in `<nav>`).
- **Toggle button:** `<button aria-pressed="true|false">` for on/off tools (bold, mute); `role="switch"` with `aria-checked` for settings switches.
- **Combobox:** complex; use a well-tested library (or native `<select>` / `<datalist>` where acceptable).
- **Tooltip:** `aria-describedby` from the trigger to the tooltip; it supplements, never replaces, an accessible name.
- **Carousels:** pause control, previous/next buttons, no auto-advance (or pause on hover/focus), each slide reachable by keyboard. Usually a carousel is the wrong pattern; show the content.

## 10. Motion and timing

- `prefers-reduced-motion`: see motion.md.
- No content flashing more than 3 times per second.
- Auto-updating, moving, or scrolling content lasting more than 5 seconds needs pause/stop/hide.
- Time limits (session timeouts, timed quizzes) must be adjustable or extendable, with a warning before expiry.

## 11. Forced colors and user preferences

- **Windows High Contrast / forced colors** replaces your colors with a system palette and removes box-shadows and background images. Test with `@media (forced-colors: active)`.
  - Use real borders (even `1px solid transparent`) on buttons, cards, and inputs so they still have edges.
  - Focus indicators should use `outline` (survives) rather than `box-shadow` (removed).
  - SVG icons using `currentColor` adapt automatically.
- Respect `prefers-color-scheme`, `prefers-reduced-motion`, `prefers-contrast: more` (strengthen borders and text), and `prefers-reduced-transparency` (replace frosted-glass effects with solid surfaces).

## 12. Testing

Automated tools catch roughly a third of issues. Do all of these:
1. **Keyboard pass:** unplug the mouse. Tab through everything. Can you see focus at all times? Reach and operate everything? Escape every overlay? Is the order logical?
2. **Automated scan:** axe DevTools, Lighthouse, or WAVE; fix all errors.
3. **Zoom:** 200% browser zoom and a 320px-wide window.
4. **Screen reader spot check:** VoiceOver (macOS: Cmd+F5; iOS), NVDA (Windows, free), or TalkBack (Android). Navigate by headings and landmarks; operate a form; open a dialog. Does what you hear match what you see?
5. **Contrast check** of text and UI states, including hover, disabled, placeholder, and dark mode.
6. **Forced colors** emulation in Chrome DevTools (Rendering panel), plus color-vision-deficiency emulation.

## 13. Snippets

```html
<!-- Skip link: first element in <body> -->
<a class="skip-link" href="#main">Skip to main content</a>
...
<main id="main" tabindex="-1">…</main>
```

```css
.skip-link {
  position: absolute; left: var(--space-4); top: var(--space-4); z-index: var(--z-tooltip);
  padding: var(--space-2) var(--space-4); background: var(--color-surface); color: var(--color-text);
  border-radius: var(--radius-md); box-shadow: var(--shadow-md);
  translate: 0 -200%;
}
.skip-link:focus-visible { translate: 0 0; }

/* Text for screen readers only */
.sr-only { position: absolute !important; width: 1px; height: 1px; padding: 0; margin: -1px; overflow: hidden; clip-path: inset(50%); white-space: nowrap; border: 0; }

/* Keep focused elements clear of a sticky header */
html { scroll-padding-top: 5rem; }

/* Strengthen boundaries when users ask for more contrast */
@media (prefers-contrast: more) {
  :root { --color-border: var(--color-border-control); --color-text-muted: var(--color-text); }
}

/* Make sure custom controls keep edges in forced colors */
@media (forced-colors: active) {
  .btn, .card, .input { border: 1px solid CanvasText; }
}
```

```html
<!-- Icon button with accessible name and tooltip -->
<button class="btn btn-ghost" aria-label="Archive" aria-describedby="tip-archive">
  <svg aria-hidden="true" focusable="false">…</svg>
</button>
<div role="tooltip" id="tip-archive">Archive (E)</div>

<!-- Field with hint and error -->
<div class="field">
  <label for="email">Work email</label>
  <input id="email" class="input" type="email" autocomplete="email" required
         aria-invalid="true" aria-describedby="email-hint email-error">
  <p class="hint" id="email-hint">We'll send the invite here.</p>
  <p class="error" id="email-error">Enter an email address like name@company.com</p>
</div>

<!-- Polite status region, present on page load -->
<div role="status" aria-live="polite" class="sr-only" id="status"></div>
```
